content:
Multiple Dropbox users received emails from the cloud storage company notifying them that their accounts had been accessed without authorization due to a security vulnerability.

The root cause appears to be that Dropbox did not set up an authentication process when attackers set up single sign-on (SSO) options through a third-party company……

Developer Yoni Levy shared the content of the email he received on social media platform X.

Other Dropbox users also said they received similar emails, mentioning that the issue occurred when setting up single sign-on (SSO) options using a Lenovo ID.

However, although Dropbox claimed the flaw lay in Lenovo's email verification process, the bigger problem seems to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to verify new SSO setups through their original sign-in method, according to The CyberSec Guru.

  • Reconnaissance and filtering: The attacker collects target email addresses (through leaked databases, LinkedIn, customer lists—email addresses are essentially public information).
  • Malicious identity provider registration: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID using victim@example.com. The process does not require access to the victim's email, because Lenovo's verification steps are either missing or can be bypassed. The display name is set to a throwaway name—one user who successfully recovered a hijacked account found the name was that of the late NFL broadcaster "John Madden," strongly suggesting a bulk, low-cost registration operation.
  • Federated login: The attacker clicks "Continue with Lenovo" on Dropbox. Lenovo's authorization server issues a token whose email claim matches the victim's Dropbox account.
  • Implicit account linking: Dropbox matches the email claim to an existing account and generates a login session. No password required, no additional verification, and no "Link this new identity?" consent prompt. From Dropbox's perspective, a trusted identity provider has vouched for that email address.

9to5Mac's take

Although Lenovo does indeed have shortcomings in email address verification, if Dropbox had performed verification before the linked identity was used to sign in, no damage would have been caused at all. Failing to do so is a serious oversight.

The company subsequently fixed the vulnerability and invalidated all previously "verified" sessions that had been authenticated through Lenovo IDs.
